stories.headline: ICE Obtains Local Voter Registration Files in Two Counties in Noncitizen Voting Probe
stories.summary:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators have obtained individual voter files directly from local election officials in two counties — one in Texas and one in North Carolina — according to emails shared with Axios. The action represents a new phase in the Trump administration's multi-agency effort to investigate alleged noncitizen voting, going beyond federal databases and reaching into state and local election systems.

President Trump has long claimed that millions of noncitizens vote illegally in U.S. elections and has used that assertion to explain his loss in the 2016 popular vote. Supporters of the effort argue it is a legitimate law enforcement exercise to protect election integrity, while critics warn that ICE accessing voter rolls sets a troubling precedent that could chill voter registration and blur the line between immigration enforcement and election administration.

The disclosure raises legal and constitutional questions about the appropriate role of immigration authorities in accessing election records, which are administered under state and local law. Election law advocates on the left argue the move could amount to voter intimidation and a federal overreach into state-controlled systems; administration allies contend existing law permits such inquiries as part of a lawful investigation into potential federal crimes.

stories.headline: Update: Anthropic Suspends Claude Fable 5 AI Model Worldwide After U.S. Government Security Order
stories.summary:
Anthropic has been ordered by U.S. national security authorities to suspend access to its most powerful AI model, Claude Fable 5, just days after its public release. The company said it was directed to bar foreign nationals from using the tool, and because it could not reliably enforce that restriction for individual users, it disabled the model entirely for all customers globally, including a related model called Mythos 5.

U.S. authorities told Anthropic they had become aware of a method for "jailbreaking" Fable 5 — bypassing its safety restrictions in ways that could allow hackers to exploit computer systems. Anthropic said it reviewed a demonstration of the technique and found the vulnerabilities to be relatively minor and already discoverable through other publicly available AI models, suggesting the company believes the government's concerns may be overstated.

The suspension adds to an already fraught relationship between Anthropic and the Trump administration. The Defense Department previously designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk" — the first time such a label, historically reserved for foreign adversaries, was applied to a U.S. company. Anthropic is currently suing the Pentagon over that designation. A federal judge has ruled the directive unenforceable in the meantime, allowing government-adjacent organizations to continue using Anthropic's other tools.

stories.headline: Justice Department Clears $111 Billion Warner Bros. Discovery Sale to Paramount
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice has approved Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, clearing a major antitrust hurdle for what would be one of the largest media mergers in history. The DOJ said it conducted a "rigorous" review and found the deal unlikely to harm competition or consumers, and predicted it would actually increase competition across the media landscape.

The combined company would control an enormous portfolio of media assets, including CNN, HBO, Warner Bros. film studios, DC Studios, CBS, Showtime, Nickelodeon, and multiple cable networks. The deal has drawn opposition from more than 1,400 Hollywood actors, directors, and filmmakers who signed an open letter warning it would reduce jobs, limit creative opportunities, raise costs, and shrink choices for audiences.

The merger is not yet final. California Attorney General Rob Bonta has been reviewing the deal and previously expressed concern that further consolidation would harm the entertainment industry; a spokesperson said the state's investigation remains open. The deal has also attracted scrutiny because Paramount is led by David Ellison, son of Oracle's Larry Ellison, a major donor to President Trump — raising questions among critics about whether political considerations influenced the DOJ's approval.

stories.headline: Shooting in Downtown Midland, Texas Kills at Least One; Suspect Dead
stories.summary:
At least one person was killed and others injured in a shooting in downtown Midland, Texas on Friday, Mayor Lori Blong announced at a press conference. The suspect, who had barricaded themselves inside a building following the shooting, was subsequently confirmed dead.

Midland police and emergency services responded to the active-shooter situation in the city's downtown area. Authorities provided limited details as the situation was still developing at the time of initial reports. The incident drew coverage from more than a dozen national news outlets.

Midland, a West Texas city of roughly 130,000 people and a center of the Permian Basin oil industry, was the site of a mass shooting in August 2019 in which a gunman killed seven people and wounded more than 20 others in a rampage across the city and neighboring Odessa. Authorities have not yet released information on a motive or the identities of those involved in Friday's incident.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Iran Deal Near Signing as Israel Strikes Lebanon, Hormuz Reopening Promised
stories.summary:
Iran's foreign minister said Friday that a deal to end hostilities with the United States is close to finalization and would include reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting a U.S. blockade of Iran. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, who helped mediate the agreement, confirmed a Memorandum of Understanding had been agreed and awaited finalizing. However, Iran's foreign minister acknowledged that the Supreme National Security Council had not yet reached a collective decision, saying "supporters and opponents" exist within Iran's top security body.

President Trump said Thursday he had cancelled scheduled strikes against Iran because negotiators had reached a "great settlement," but then disputed details published by Iranian media, saying the leaked terms "bear no relation to the truth." U.S. officials confirmed some elements of the deal, stating that economic benefits for Iran would be contingent on Tehran meeting its obligations. The agreement is also said to envision an end to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict in Lebanon, though Lebanon's inclusion has been disputed in earlier reports.

Israel carried out fresh airstrikes in southern Lebanon on Friday after ordering residents to evacuate roughly 20 locations, with at least one person killed in the Tyre district town of Marrakeh. The strikes came hours after Iran's foreign minister outlined deal terms, underscoring the fragility of the broader ceasefire framework. Iran has previously warned Israel it could resume hostilities if attacks on Hezbollah do not stop.

The ongoing conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, has closed the Strait of Hormuz and trapped an estimated 20,000 seafarers in the war zone. BBC Verify analysis of satellite imagery found Iran has damaged 20 U.S. military sites since the war began, more than publicly acknowledged. The deal's nuclear components — long a central Western concern — are reportedly deferred to later negotiations.

stories.headline: U.S. Military Kills Tren de Aragua Gang Leader Niño Guerrero in Airstrike
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that U.S. Southern Command carried out a lethal airstrike killing Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, known as Niño Guerrero, the longtime leader of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. Trump posted footage of the strike on social media and said the operation was "coordinated closely" with Venezuelan authorities, who confirmed their participation in what they called a "joint operation." The Trump administration had previously designated Tren de Aragua a foreign terrorist organization and accused it of engaging in "irregular warfare" against the United States.

Tren de Aragua originated as a prison gang in Venezuela that Guerrero transformed into a transnational criminal organization with operations in at least nine countries, including the United States. Under his leadership, the group expanded into Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Chile, diversifying from extorting migrants into sex trafficking, contract killing, and kidnapping. The U.S. State Department had offered millions of dollars for information leading to his arrest or capture.

The killing comes amid a significant reshaping of U.S.-Venezuela relations. In January, American forces seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in a raid; Guerrero Flores had been named as a co-conspirator in Maduro's U.S. indictment. Since Maduro's removal, the U.S. has worked to build ties with his successor, Delcy Rodríguez, including lifting sanctions and pursuing collaboration on Venezuela's vast oil reserves.

Guerrero had a long history of escaping accountability, including bribing a guard to escape prison in 2012 and evading capture again in 2023 when Maduro sent 11,000 soldiers to retake the Tocorón Prison — which Guerrero had transformed into a compound complete with a zoo, nightclub, and swimming pool. His death marks the most significant targeted strike against a Latin American criminal organization's leadership under the Trump administration.

stories.headline: Update: FISA Section 702 Expires as Congress Deadlocks Over Trump Intelligence Nominee
stories.summary:
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, one of the U.S. government's most powerful foreign surveillance tools, lapsed this weekend after Congress failed to reauthorize it. Democrats blocked extension votes in both chambers in protest of President Trump's nomination of Housing Secretary Bill Pulte to temporarily oversee the nation's intelligence services. The standoff leaves the fate of ongoing intelligence collection in legal uncertainty, with the law's expiration coming days before the 2026 World Cup, which U.S. security officials have flagged as a heightened terrorism target.

Lawmakers and legal experts are divided on the practical consequences of the lapse. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) argued that thousands of existing FISA certifications remain valid and that the expiration does not immediately end U.S. surveillance of foreign terrorists. However, Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, warned the situation was "a high-risk proposition," raising the possibility that telecom and tech companies such as Google could decline to cooperate with intelligence requests without explicit congressional authorization.

Section 702 allows the government to collect communications of foreign nationals abroad using U.S. infrastructure, though it also incidentally captures communications of Americans in contact with foreign suspects — a provision that has long troubled privacy advocates in both parties. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) placed blame on the Trump administration, saying it had "tossed a hand grenade into the middle of sensitive negotiations" by installing Pulte. Republicans countered that Democrats were endangering national security for political reasons.

The program had previously been credited with disrupting domestic terror plots. A resolution is not expected soon, as Trump has shown no indication he will withdraw the Pulte nomination, and Democrats have not signaled any willingness to relent without a concession.

stories.headline: Switzerland Votes Sunday on Unprecedented Referendum to Cap Population at 10 Million
stories.summary:
Swiss voters will go to the polls Sunday on a proposal backed by the right-wing Swiss People's Party to constitutionally cap the country's population at 10 million residents before 2050, with mandatory government action once the population reaches 9.5 million. Proposed measures to enforce the cap could include limiting asylum grants and ending family reunification for foreign residents. Switzerland's population has grown from 7.3 million in 2002 to 9.1 million today, with 27 percent of residents being foreign nationals.

The Swiss government, all major opposition parties, business groups, and trade unions have united against the measure, calling it a "chaos initiative" that would deprive hospitals and hotels of essential workers and damage Switzerland's carefully maintained bilateral relations with the European Union, of which it is not a member. Supporters argue unchecked immigration has driven a housing shortage, overcrowded trains, and rising healthcare costs. No other country has attempted a hard constitutional cap on population.

Polling shows the vote is extremely close, with roughly 52 percent of respondents opposed and 45 percent in favor, while a significant share of voters remain undecided. The outcome could have significant implications for Switzerland's relationship with the EU, its labor market, and its reputation as a destination for international workers and talent.
